title: From scalar loops to array operations
summary: Array languages, episode 2: map, filter and reduce as whole-array operations in place of a loop, a mask to filter and to count, Rust iterator chains compared, and three steps composed.

scenes.heading: From scalar loops to array operations
Three kinds of loop
scenes.narration: In the last episode, we compared a loop with a whole array operation. In this episode{,|/} we turn common {loops|loops /} into array operations. Three kinds come up again and again. Map, filter, and reduce.

scenes.heading: One loop, three jobs
scenes.narration: Here is a small Rust loop. It takes the values two, four, six, eight. It triples each value. It keeps the ones greater than five. And it adds up what it keeps. Three jobs are tangled together in one loop body.

scenes.heading: How, or what
scenes.narration: {Scalar|@scalar} style code {describes|describes /} how to visit every element. Array style code describes what happens to the whole collection.

items.sub: visit every element, one at a time
what happens to the whole collection

scenes.heading: Map
scenes.narration: The first job is a map. Three times values gives six, twelve, eighteen, twenty four. Every input element produces one output element. The shape stays the same.

scenes.heading: Tripled
scenes.narration: {X_eTaL|@xtl} says it in one line. Tripled is three times values. There is no loop, and no index.

scenes.heading: Filter: a question for every element
scenes.narration: The second job is a filter. First, we ask every element the same question. We ask if it is greater than five. The answer is zero, zero, one, one. That is a mask. One means keep, and zero means drop.

scenes.heading: Replicate
scenes.narration: Replicate uses the mask to choose. Each value is kept as many times as its mask says. So the result is six, eight. The output is shorter than the input. That is what makes a filter different from a map.

scenes.heading: Reduce
scenes.narration: The third {job|job /} is a reduce. A reduce combines many elements into one. Reduce, given plus, adds them up, and gives twenty. Given max, it gives the largest value, eight. {Min|@min}{,|/} in place of max{,|/} gives the smallest value{,|/} which is two.

scenes.heading: Counting with a mask
scenes.narration: Masks and reduce work well together. A comparison gives ones and zeros. Adding them up counts the matches. So two values are greater than five. Reduce, given and, asks whether every value passes. Every value is greater than one, so it gives one.

scenes.heading: Iterator chains
scenes.narration: Modern languages can describe this too. Rust has iterator chains. Map, then filter, then sum. The difference is not that Rust cannot map or reduce. In an array language, arrays and their operations are the center of the language.

scenes.heading: Three steps, composed
scenes.narration: Now we put the three together. Triple the values. Keep the ones greater than five. Add them up. The answer is sixty, the same as the loop. Each step is one whole array operation, and each one has a name.

scenes.heading: Next: shape, rank, axes
scenes.narration: The next episode is about the shape of an array{,|/} its rank{,|/} and its {axes|@axes}. Here is a short preview.

scenes.heading: Shape
scenes.narration: Shape says how long each axis is. The shape of a list of five values is five. A table with three rows and four columns has shape three by four. It holds twelve values. Multiply the lengths in a shape{,|/} and you get the number of values. A shape is a short list of numbers{,|/} one for each axis.

scenes.heading: Rank
scenes.narration: Rank is the number of {axes|@axes}. A single value{,|/} called a {scalar|@scalar}{,|/} has rank zero. A list has rank one. A table has rank two{,|/} not twelve. Add another axis{,|/} and the rank is three. The rank tells us how many {axes|@axes} there are. The shape tells us how long each one is.

scenes.heading: Axes
scenes.narration: An axis is one direction through an array. A table has two{,|/} down the rows{,|/} and across the columns. Reduce can add along either one. Down the rows gives a total for each column. Across the columns gives a total for each row. The shape of an array decides which operations make sense.

scenes.heading: Before the next episode
scenes.narration: Before the next episode, try this. Take a list of temperatures in Fahrenheit. Change each one to Celsius. Keep the ones below freezing. Then count them. Try to describe all of that without a loop.
